title: Lossless Reductions and Hybrid Sampling for Phylogeny Using the Maximum Compatibility Criterion
authors: Orson Ye, James Bonfield, Joshua Cudby, Richard Durbin, Sergii Strelchuk
abstract: Maximum compatibility provides a criterion for phylogenetic reconstruction in which the objective is to retain a maximum set of mutually compatible characters. For binary characters, pairwise compatibility can be represented by a weighted graph whose vertices correspond to characters and whose edges connect compatible pairs. A leading algorithm by Cherry [BMC Bioinformatics, 18(1):127, 2017] uses this representation to identify maximum compatible character sets as maximum weight cliques.   We formulate the problem as maximum weight independent set enumeration on the complement graph and use deterministic postprocessing to map sampled bit strings to maximal feasible solutions. To explore the prospects of quantum computational advantage, we further construct bespoke correction-in-the-loop Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm instances and find that traditional Lagrange multiplier choices may not be optimal for the enumeration problem on noisy devices.   We also introduce lossless graph reductions with reconstruction rules that preserve the complete set of optimal solutions. Our results indicate that graph reduction and sampling can be effectively combined to address the enumeration bottleneck in maximum compatibility phylogeny, while retaining exact reconstruction when the residual optimum set is completely resolved.   We enhance Cherry's approach to maximum compatibility by introducing graph reduction techniques and quantum sampling. Our classical benchmarks show a clear difference between finding one optimum and recovering the optimum set in practice. We demonstrate the utility of our methods on graphs constructed from SARS-CoV-2 sequences.
summary: This paper enhances phylogenetic reconstruction by tackling the difficult problem of enumerating all maximum compatible character sets. It combines graph reduction techniques with quantum sampling methods and benchmarks these against advanced classical solvers. The goal is to efficiently solve the underlying maximum weight clique problem derived from sequence compatibility data.
main_problem: The paper addresses the computationally hard problem of enumerating all maximum weight cliques (MWC) derived from the Maximum Compatibility Criterion used in phylogenetic reconstruction.
main_result: The authors propose a hybrid approach combining graph reduction techniques with quantum sampling and advanced classical solvers to tackle the enumeration bottleneck, showing improvements over existing methods.
method: The methodology involves formulating the problem as a maximum weight independent set enumeration, applying lossless graph reductions, and testing bespoke Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm (QAOA) instances alongside classical solvers like AClique and SCCWalk4L.
model_or_system: The model is phylogenetic reconstruction based on Multiple Sequence Alignments (MSAs), where compatibility data forms a weighted graph whose MWC corresponds to the optimal set of characters retained.
key_observables: The primary observables are the size and weight of the maximum compatible character set (MWC), and the computational time required to enumerate the entire set of optimal solutions.
important_parameters: Graph size (number of vertices/characters), weights assigned to characters, and the number of samples/iterations used in quantum algorithms.
main_assumptions: The work assumes that graph reduction and quantum sampling can be effectively combined to maintain exact reconstruction, although the quantum results are not claimed as a definitive quantum advantage.
figures_summary: Figures benchmark various classical solvers (FastWCLQ2, SCCWalk4L, AClique) showing the trade-off between computational time and the quality (size) of the found maximum clique for graphs of increasing size.
paper_structure: The paper builds upon existing work (Cherry's algorithm), first detailing the formulation as an MWC enumeration problem, then introducing graph reduction techniques, and finally exploring hybrid solvers combining these reductions with quantum sampling and benchmarking against state-of-the-art classical solvers.
why_interesting: While the core problem is combinatorial biology, the explicit formulation of the MWC problem as a QUBO/MWIS problem and the application of QAOA instances make it relevant to quantum algorithm development for hard optimization problems.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: Benchmarks of exact maximum clique solvers, IncMaxCLQ and CliSAT. The results derived from graphs taken from random subsets of size 100 to 20,000 sequences in increments of 50. Times are the total execution time.

Figure 1 shows the time taken as a function of the number of nodes in the graph. Both CliSAT and IncMaxCLQ show a polynomial base-line for CPU growth, which can cover the bulk of the execution runs. However there are outliers which are expected to follow an exponential CPU growth. The tools can be ran with a fixed time limit, returning the best result found within that time.

Figure 2: Benchmarks of the approximate solver SCCWalk4L. This returns a single clique after a time limit of 1000s. Colours represent the quality of result, showing perfect maximum cliques, imperfect cliques found with at least 99% of the maximum clique size, and cliques found below 99%. Times shown are the time to find the best solution, which is typically considerably less than the fixed specified execution time.
Figure 3: Scatter plots of the depth and gate count against number of qubits of the QAOA circuits required to solve the MWC problem on various subsets of SARS-CoV-2 genome samples.

Figure 4: For different Lagrange multipliers, the low energy solutions correspond to different subgraphs. Taking different fractions of the lowest energies, we show what proportions of the corresponding subgraphs correspond to MWCs given our postprocessing algorithm.
